title: Unit Conversion Precision: Float Error and Significant Digits
description: Slightly off conversions are rarely miscalculated: area squares a ratio, temperature is an offset, storage uses 1024, mu, months and years are approximations.
content:
A conversion result that comes out slightly off from what you expected is usually not the tool doing the arithmetic wrong. Three things stack up instead: double-precision floating point can only approximate most decimal fractions, area and volume need a linear ratio squared or cubed, and the mu, the month and the year rest on agreed constants. The sections below take them in implementation order and mark which differences you should fix and which you should accept.

I. There Are Only Two Conversion Models: Multiply a Ratio, or Add an Offset

The unit converter on this site covers six categories and 37 units: 8 for length, 7 for weight, 3 for temperature, 6 for data storage, 8 for time and 5 for area. Except for temperature, every unit carries a single factor against a base unit, so a conversion is a multiplication by the source ratio followed by a division by the target ratio.

Take 100 kilometres to miles: 100×1000÷1609.344. The mile factor is 1609.344, so two floating-point operations each appear once; length, weight, storage, time and area all travel this path.

Temperature has no factor. toBase folds the input back to degrees Celsius: Fahrenheit subtracts 32 and divides by 1.8, Kelvin simply subtracts 273.15. fromBase reverses it by multiplying by 1.8 and adding 32, or by adding 273.15. Offset and ratio sit in one formula, so the error surface gains an extra layer.

Every symptom later in this article belongs to one of three classes: a ratio that was squared or cubed, an offset that took an approximate value, or a residual left behind when two floating-point numbers are divided.

II. Where Floating-Point Error Comes From: Double Precision and Every Rounding Step

JavaScript's Number has exactly one representation: the IEEE 754 double-precision 64-bit binary floating-point format (binary64). MDN's Number page states that this is a 64-bit double-precision binary format; the largest consecutive integer it represents exactly is 2 to the 53rd power minus one, that is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 9007199254740991. The decimal fraction 0.1 is a repeating fraction in binary and can only be stored as an approximation, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 yields 0.30000000000000004 rather than 0.3.

How large is the residual? Number.EPSILON is 2.220446049250313e-16, the gap between 1 and the smallest representable number greater than 1, which you can read as the double-precision tick near 1. 0.1 + 0.2 − 0.3 gives 5.551115123125783e-17, an order of magnitude that lands right on this tick: the error is about 0.25 EPSILON, one tick near 0.3, not a calculation error. MDN also gives the mantissa precision as 2 to the −52, roughly 15 to 17 decimal significant digits; anything finer is rounded away.

Temperature conversion shows it directly. 37 °C runs value * 1.8 + 32: 37×1.8 first yields 66.60000000000001, and adding 32 yields 98.60000000000001.

Nor is a residual guaranteed: 1 inch to centimetres is 0.0254÷0.01, and the double-precision result is exactly 2.54. So "floating point" is not a catch-all explanation; what matters is where those two operations land.

III. 12 Significant Digits: The Tail Is Clipped, and the Cost Is Truncation

The displayed value is not the raw result. After the script has result it runs Number(result.toPrecision(12)).toString(): take 12 significant digits, convert back to a number to drop the padding zeros, then print the shortest form. The three steps together turn 98.60000000000001 into 98.6.

The same display rule is used in the scientific calculator, where 1÷3 shows as 0.333333333333. 12 digits is the display setting those two tools share.

ConversionInternal valueDisplayed valueSource of the difference
37 °C → °F98.6000000000000198.6residual hidden by 12 digits
100 °F → °C37.7777777777777837.7777777778truncated to 12 significant digits
100 km → miles62.1371192237333962.1371192237same as above
3 mu → square metres2000.00012000.0001residual on the 8th digit, which 12 digits cannot hide
1 PB → bytes11258999068426241125899906840000exact value truncated

"Significant digits" is not "decimal places": 1 kilogram to pounds shows 2.20462262185, 11 digits after the point; 1 GB to bytes shows 1073741824, 10 digits with no point at all.

In the other direction, exact values are truncated by the same 12 digits. In storage the factor for 1 PB is 2 to the 50th, that is 1125899906842624 bytes, but the display reads 1125899906840000; the exact value of 9 PB, 10133099161583616, displays as 10133099161600000. This is not a floating-point residual; the display rule is deliberately dropping digits.

Both directions together give the full conclusion: 12 digits hides residuals and truncates over-long exact values alike, so for any result beyond 12 significant digits, suspect the display before you suspect the computation.

IV. Area Squares the Ratio; Volume Cubes It

Ratios go length against length, so area and volume cannot reuse them as they are. Converting square metres to square feet, the linear ratio of the foot is 0.3048 metres, so the area ratio is 0.3048 squared, 0.09290304; in the code the factor for ft2 is exactly 0.09290304, bit-identical in double precision to the square of 0.3048.

Hence 1 square metre = 1÷0.09290304 = 10.7639104167 square feet. Divide by 0.3048 on its own and you get about 3.28, which converts a length rather than an area.

Volume needs more care: the tool has no volume category. Converting 1 cubic foot means cubing it yourself; 0.3048 cubed is 0.028316846592000004, which at 12 significant digits is written 0.028316846592 cubic metres; and 1 cubic metre = 1000 litres.

In the same way, speed is length divided by time and density is mass divided by volume; no single ratio covers either.

V. Temperature Is an Offset, Not a Ratio

Temperature runs differently from length: 0 °C is not 0 °F, because the two scales differ in origin as well as step size. In the code Fahrenheit is first folded back with (value − 32) / 1.8 and then converted outward; Celsius and Kelvin differ only by 273.15, a pure translation.

The four points on the page can be checked directly: 37 °C = 98.6 °F; 100 °F = 37.7777777778 °C; −40 °C = −40 °F, the only point where the two scales coincide; and −300 °C = −26.85 K.

The last one deserves a note: absolute zero is −273.15 °C, and the tool does not validate physical range, so anything below it still produces a negative Kelvin value. Conversion only changes scales; physical meaning is for the user to judge.

The result area shows only 98.6, without the 98.60000000000001 tail; that is the 12-digit formatting from section III at work, not precision in the arithmetic itself.

VI. Data Size: 1024 and 1000 Are Two Different Prefix Systems

Storage units start the most arguments. The BIPM SI prefix table defines decimal prefixes: k is 10 to the 3rd, M is 10 to the 6th, G is 10 to the 9th. NIST's "Prefixes for binary multiples" sets binary prefixes up separately: Ki is 2 to the 10th, that is 1024, with Mi and Gi following at 2 to the 20th and 2 to the 30th, and it gives the comparisons 1 MiB = 1 048 576 B and 1 GiB = 1 073 741 824 B.

In the tool, B, KB, MB, GB, TB and PB all step by powers of 2: 1 KB = 1024 B, 1 MB = 1048576 B, 1 GB = 1073741824 B, 1 TB = 1099511627776 B, 1 PB = 1125899906842624 B. The interface says "KB" while the arithmetic is really KiB.

UnitBytesPower of 2Strict name
B12^0byte
KB10242^10KiB
MB10485762^20MiB
GB10737418242^30GiB
TB10995116277762^40TiB
PB11258999068426242^50PiB

So: 1 GB to MB displays 1024; 1000 B to KB displays 0.9765625, because 1000÷1024. A drive vendor's 1 TB counts 10 to the 12th bytes, and read as 2 to the 40th it is only about 0.9095 TB, a gap of about 9.05%. Two numbers for one disk come from two prefix systems.

Go further and you reach the double-precision ceiling: exact consecutive integers run to 2 to the 53rd minus one, that is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 9007199254740991. 1 PB is 2 to the 50th bytes and 8 PB is exactly 2 to the 53rd bytes; past 8 PB an increment of 1 byte is rounded away and may leave the value where it was or jump to the next representable one, so 9 PB plus 1 still equals 9 PB. Stack the display truncation on top and PB-scale byte counts can only be read as approximations; for byte-exact work use integer arithmetic or the base converter.

VII. Approximate Constants: Mu, Month and Year

Some units have no exact decimal value, so the data can only hold an approximate constant. The factor for the mu (亩) is 666.6667, while the common conversion is 1 mu = 1/15 hectare = 666.666… square metres, which does not divide evenly. Substituting 666.6667 leaves a relative error of about 5e-8.

The error is small, but multiply it by a large number and it shows: 3 mu should equal 2000 square metres and the tool displays 2000.0001. That 0.0001 is not absorbed the way 98.6 was, because it sits on the 8th significant digit and 12 digits have room for it.

The two time constants are even more explicit: a month is fixed at 2592000 seconds, that is 30 days, and a year at 31536000 seconds, that is 365 days, and the unit labels spell out the 30-day month and the 365-day year. Hence 1 year = 12.1666666667 months; 4 years = 1460 days, while four Gregorian calendar years usually hold 1461 days, because the leap day is swallowed by that convention.

These are approximations for bookkeeping and estimation, not astronomical constants. Contract terms, interest across months and reports counted by calendar month must be worked out again from the agreed start and end dates; a conversion result cannot serve directly as a settlement basis.

VIII. Significant Digits and Rounding: Display Precision Is Not Internal Precision

12 significant digits is a display rule, not a count of trustworthy digits. Convert a measurement such as 1.2 metres, which carries two significant digits, and the result still prints a long string of digits, but it must not be read as 12-digit precision; how many you keep depends on the significant digits of the source data and on business rules. Writing adds another rule: NIST SP 811 section 7.2 requires a space between a numerical value and its unit symbol, including before the degree-Celsius symbol, so write 30.2 °C rather than 30.2°C.

For business rounding you have to settle three things yourself: which place to round to, which rule to use (half-up, truncation, banker's rounding), and at which step to round. The common mistake is rounding at every step, so errors accumulate; the steadier approach keeps full precision in the middle and rounds once, on the final output.

Money is the classic case. The RMB uppercase converter first rounds the amount to fen with Math.round(input * 100) / 100, takes the absolute value with Math.abs, then converts to uppercase. That pattern breaks on 1.005: the double-precision value of 1.005 is about 1.00499999999999989, so multiplying by 100 gives 100.49999999999999, and Math.round yields 100 — the output is 「壹元整」 (one whole yuan) instead of the expected one whole yuan plus one fen. To carry by decimal rules, split the amount into integer fen as a string first, then round.

Likewise toFixed(2) is not rounding either: it works on the actual binary value, and edge cases such as 1.005 also fail to give 1.01. Auditable amounts need integer fen or a decimal library.

IX. Boundaries and Limits

Listing the boundaries plainly is more useful than memorising numbers:

  • Six categories and 37 units only — length, weight, temperature, data storage, time and area; no volume, speed, pressure, energy or currency.
  • Temperature is not physically validated: −300 °C still computes −26.85 K, with no warning below absolute zero.
  • Storage steps by powers of 1024 yet is named KB, MB, GB; to align with a vendor's decimal figures you must convert powers of 1000 yourself.
  • The mu, the month and the year are approximate or agreed constants, so results must not go straight into contracts and settlements.
  • Display is trimmed to 12 significant digits, which both hides residuals and truncates over-long exact values; PB-scale byte counts can only be read as approximations.
  • The input is type="number": it accepts forms such as 1e3 and echoes 1000 in the result area, taking only digits and exponent notation; an empty or non-finite value shows 「请输入有效数值」 (enter a valid number), the result switches to a dash, the unit and source lines empty out, and the copy-result button is disabled.
  • The first line of the result area echoes the parsed value: typing 1.50 shows 1.5 millimetres; switching category defaults to Fahrenheit for temperature and to the second unit for the others.

Ratio arithmetic with decimals leaves floating-point residuals; integer-only base conversion is untouched by that layer: the base converter accumulates digit by digit with BigInt, 1024 from decimal to hexadecimal gives 400, exactly 2 to the 10th, and 1152921504606846976 to hexadecimal gives 1000000000000000, not a digit off.

X. Common Misconceptions

  • "12 significant digits means the result is exact": it is only a display setting; 98.6 masks 98.60000000000001, and 1125899906840000 masks the exact 1125899906842624.
  • "1 GB = 1024 MB is the international standard": the SI gigabyte is 10 to the 9th bytes; the 1024-based set is the binary prefixes KiB, MiB, GiB, and the tool uses the latter's values with the former's names.
  • "The mu is an integer unit": 1 mu = 1/15 hectare, which does not divide evenly; the tool approximates with 666.6667, so 3 mu comes out 0.0001 over.
  • "A conversion result can go straight into a contract": the mu, the month, the year and the storage convention all carry agreements; formal work needs the standard the project specifies and a review step.

faqs.q: Why does 37 °C display as 98.6 rather than 98.60000000000001?
faqs.a: The arithmetic does produce 98.60000000000001; before display the value is taken to 12 significant digits and then printed in its shortest form, so the tail is clipped. Twelve digits is a display rule, not a promise of precision.

faqs.q: Why is 3 mu not exactly 2000 square metres?
faqs.a: 1 mu = 1/15 hectare = 666.666… square metres, which does not divide evenly; the tool uses the approximate constant 666.6667, so 3 mu comes out as 2000.0001. For an exact figure compute 10000/15 yourself, or round by the project standard.

faqs.q: How many MB is 1 GB, exactly?
faqs.a: The tool counts in powers of 2, so 1 GB = 1024 MB; under the SI decimal convention 1 GB = 1000 MB. The former matches the values of the strict names GiB and MiB, while the interface keeps the GB and MB names.

faqs.q: Can a conversion result go straight into a contract or a settlement?
faqs.a: Not advisable. The mu, the month and the year are approximate or agreed constants, storage runs on two prefix systems, and the display is truncated at 12 significant digits; formal work needs the convention stated, rounding by agreement and a review.
